questions.q: Explain defence in depth, least privilege, secure defaults and fail closed by showing how each changes a concrete design for a payments API.
questions.a:
### Defence in depth
Multiple independent controls so one failure doesn't mean compromise: WAF and gateway validation, token validation in the service, object-level authorisation, parameterised queries, database permissions, encryption at rest, monitoring. An attacker must defeat several layers.

### Least privilege
Every identity gets only what it needs: the payments API's database user can execute specific stored procedures or DML on its own schema (no DDL, no access to other schemas); its managed identity reads only its own Key Vault secrets; engineers have no standing production access.

### Secure defaults
New endpoints require authentication unless explicitly marked anonymous; CORS closed by default; TLS everywhere; headers set by middleware; templates ship with these defaults so teams don't opt in.

### Fail closed
When a security dependency fails, deny rather than allow: if the authorisation service is unreachable, reject the payment rather than skipping the check; if signature verification throws, treat as invalid. (Distinguish from availability controls like rate limiters where fail-open may be justified.)

### Also
Separation of duties, minimise attack surface (remove unused endpoints and ports), and "assume breach" thinking: what can an attacker do from here?
pts: Defence in depth: independent layers.
Least privilege for services, data and people.
Secure defaults so teams don't opt in.
Fail closed for security checks.
Assume breach; minimise attack surface.
questions.ex: A team's entitlement check returned "allowed" on timeout to keep payments flowing; during an entitlement-service outage, junior staff approved high-value payments they weren't authorised for. Fail-closed handling and a fallback policy fixed it.

questions.q: How does SQL injection work, and where can it still happen in a .NET codebase using EF Core and Dapper?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
User input is concatenated into a query so it changes the query's structure: {{' OR 1=1 --}} turns a filter into "all rows"; stacked queries can modify data. The fix is to keep data and code separate: **parameters**.

### Safe by default
- EF Core LINQ queries are parameterised.
- {{FromSql}} and {{ExecuteSql}} with **interpolated strings** are parameterised (the interpolation becomes parameters).
- Dapper with anonymous parameter objects.

### Still vulnerable
| Pattern | Problem |
|---|---|
| {{FromSqlRaw}} / {{ExecuteSqlRaw}} with concatenated strings | raw SQL injection |
| Building {{ORDER BY}} or column names from input | identifiers can't be parameterised |
| Dynamic {{LIKE}} patterns built by concatenation | injection and wildcard abuse |
| Stored procedures using dynamic SQL ({{EXEC(@sql)}}) internally | injection moves into the database |
| Dapper with string interpolation instead of parameters | concatenation |

### Identifiers
Allow-list column and direction values ({{switch}} mapping) rather than escaping.

### Defence in depth
Least-privilege database users, no {{xp_cmdshell}}, monitoring of unusual query errors.
pts: Injection changes query structure via concatenated input.
Parameters separate data from code.
EF LINQ and interpolated FromSql are safe; Raw with concatenation is not.
Allow-list identifiers like ORDER BY columns.
Dynamic SQL inside stored procedures is also vulnerable.
questions.ex: A reporting endpoint built ORDER BY from a query string; a pen tester used it to exfiltrate data via error-based injection. Replacing it with an allow-list switch closed the hole, and a Roslyn analyzer now flags FromSqlRaw with non-constant strings.

questions.q: Explain stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS. How do Angular and React protect you, and where can developers still introduce XSS?
questions.a:
### Types
| Type | How |
|---|---|
| **Stored** | malicious script saved (payee name, comment) and rendered to other users |
| **Reflected** | script in a URL parameter echoed into the page |
| **DOM-based** | client-side code writes untrusted data into dangerous sinks ({{innerHTML}}, {{eval}}, {{location}}) |
Impact: session theft (if tokens accessible), actions on behalf of the user, keylogging, phishing overlays.

### Framework protection
- **Angular**: interpolation and property binding are escaped; {{[innerHTML]}} is sanitised by the DomSanitizer; URLs sanitised.
- **React**: JSX escapes values; no HTML parsing unless {{dangerouslySetInnerHTML}}.

### Where XSS still appears
- Angular {{bypassSecurityTrustHtml}} or React {{dangerouslySetInnerHTML}} with user data.
- Direct DOM manipulation ({{ElementRef.nativeElement.innerHTML}}, jQuery plugins).
- {{href}} or {{src}} with {{javascript:}} URLs (React warns; validate URL schemes).
- Server-rendered pages (Razor with {{@Html.Raw}}).
- Third-party scripts and markdown renderers.

### Defence in depth
**Content Security Policy** with nonces or hashes (no {{unsafe-inline}}), trusted types, HttpOnly cookies, and output encoding on the server.
pts: Stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS.
Angular and React escape by default.
Bypass APIs and dangerouslySetInnerHTML reintroduce XSS.
Validate URL schemes; avoid direct DOM writes.
CSP with nonces and HttpOnly cookies as defence in depth.
questions.ex: A bank's back-office Angular app used bypassSecurityTrustHtml to render rich-text payment notes; a malicious note entered via the public API executed in staff browsers. Removing the bypass and adding a strict CSP contained the issue.

questions.q: How does CSRF work, why do SameSite cookies mostly mitigate it, and when do you still need anti-forgery tokens?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
The browser automatically attaches cookies to requests to a site, even when the request is triggered by another site. A malicious page submits a form to {{bank.example/transfer}}; the victim's session cookie goes along; the bank sees an authenticated request.

### Mitigations
| Mitigation | How it helps | Gaps |
|---|---|---|
| **SameSite=Lax** (browser default for most) | cookies not sent on cross-site POSTs | top-level GET navigations still send cookies (state-changing GETs are vulnerable); same-site subdomains can attack |
| **SameSite=Strict** | not sent on any cross-site request | users following links arrive logged out |
| **Anti-forgery tokens** | request must include a token the attacker can't read | needs integration in forms and SPAs |
| **Custom header requirement** (for example {{X-CSRF: 1}}) | cross-site forms can't set custom headers without CORS preflight | requires strict CORS |
| **Origin/Referer checks** | reject requests from unexpected origins | header may be absent |

### When tokens are still needed
Cookie-authenticated apps with sibling subdomains you don't fully control, older browsers, state-changing GETs (fix those anyway), or compliance requirements. APIs using bearer tokens in Authorization headers are not CSRF-prone (browsers don't add them automatically).
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Victim browser, logged in to bank
  participant E as Evil site
  participant B as Bank API
  U->>E: visits page with hidden auto-submitting form
  E-->>U: form posts to bank transfer endpoint
  U->>B: POST /transfers with session cookie attached
  Note over U,B: SameSite=Lax or Strict - cookie NOT sent on cross-site POST
  Note over U,B: Anti-forgery token missing or wrong - request rejected
  B-->>U: 400 or 403, no transfer
pts: Browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests.
SameSite Lax or Strict blocks most CSRF.
Anti-forgery tokens or custom headers for remaining gaps.
Never change state on GET.
Bearer-token APIs aren't CSRF-prone.
questions.ex: An internal admin app used GET /users/{id}/disable links; an attacker embedded an image tag pointing at it in a support ticket, disabling accounts when staff viewed the ticket. Moving to POST with antiforgery tokens closed it.

questions.q: Hashing vs encryption vs encoding: when do you use each? How should passwords be stored, and why are SHA-256 hashes of passwords wrong?
questions.a:
| Operation | Reversible | Key | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoding** (Base64, URL) | yes, by anyone | none | transport format; never security |
| **Encryption** (AES-GCM, RSA-OAEP) | yes, with key | yes | confidentiality of data you must read back (account numbers, documents) |
| **Hashing** (SHA-256) | no | none | integrity, fingerprints, deduplication |
| **Password hashing** (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2) | no | per-user salt, tunable cost | storing passwords |
| **MAC** (HMAC-SHA256) | no | shared secret | authenticity and integrity of messages |

### Why not SHA-256 for passwords
Fast hashes allow billions of guesses per second on GPUs; unsalted hashes allow rainbow tables and reveal identical passwords. Password hashing functions are **deliberately slow and memory-hard** with a unique salt per password.

### Recommendations
- Argon2id (memory-hard) or PBKDF2 with high iterations (ASP.NET Core Identity's PasswordHasher uses PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 and 100,000 iterations in recent versions).
- Optional **pepper** (secret key held in an HSM or Key Vault) applied with HMAC.
- Rehash on login when parameters are upgraded.
- Better still: reduce password reliance (passkeys, federated identity).
pts: Encoding isn't security; encryption is reversible with a key; hashing isn't reversible.
Passwords need slow, salted, memory-hard functions.
Argon2id or high-iteration PBKDF2.
Rehash on login when upgrading parameters.
Prefer passkeys and federation where possible.
questions.ex: A breached legacy system stored unsalted SHA-1 passwords; 70% were cracked within a day. The replacement used Identity's PBKDF2 with rehash-on-login and offered passkeys; after a year, 40% of users had no password at all.

questions.q: What is BOLA/IDOR, why is it the top API risk, and how do you structurally prevent it in an ASP.NET Core service?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
The API authenticates the caller but doesn't check that the caller may access **the specific object**: {{GET /accounts/1002}} returns someone else's account if the code only checks "is logged in". Sequential or guessable ids make enumeration trivial, but random GUIDs are **not** a fix (ids leak in URLs, logs, referrers).

### Structural prevention
1. **Scope queries by the principal**: fetch with {{WHERE Id = @id AND OwnerId = @currentUser}}; if not found, return 404 (don't reveal existence).
2. **Resource-based authorisation**: ASP.NET Core {{IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, requirement)}} with handlers encapsulating rules (owner, delegate, support role with reason).
3. **Global query filters** for tenancy (EF Core {{HasQueryFilter}}) so forgetting a filter is hard.
4. **Tests**: automated BOLA tests per endpoint (user A tries user B's ids).
5. Review checklist: every endpoint taking an id must show where ownership is checked.

### Related
Broken function-level authorisation (normal user calling admin endpoints) and property-level (seeing or setting fields they shouldn't).
pts: BOLA: authenticated but not authorised for the object.
GUIDs don't fix it.
Scope queries by principal; return 404.
Resource-based authorisation handlers.
Global tenant filters and automated BOLA tests.
questions.ex: A fintech's statement endpoint checked authentication only; a researcher downloaded 4,000 statements by iterating ids. After adding resource-based handlers and BOLA tests for every id-taking endpoint, two more vulnerable endpoints were found in other services within a week.
fu: 404 or 403 for unauthorised objects?
How do you test BOLA automatically?
How do delegated access rules fit?
pit: Checking ownership only in the UI.
Gateways assumed to handle object authorisation.

questions.q: Which HTTP security headers matter for a banking web app and API, what does each prevent, and how do you roll out CSP safely?
questions.a:
| Header | Prevents |
|---|---|
| {{Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload}} | protocol downgrade, cookie theft over HTTP |
| {{Content-Security-Policy}} | XSS impact, data exfiltration to unknown hosts, clickjacking ({{frame-ancestors}}) |
| {{X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff}} | MIME sniffing of responses as scripts |
| {{Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin}} (or no-referrer) | leaking URLs with ids to third parties |
| {{Permissions-Policy}} | unnecessary access to camera, geolocation, payment APIs |
| {{Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin}} | cross-window attacks |
| {{Cache-Control: no-store}} on sensitive responses | sensitive data in shared caches and browser history |
| {{X-Frame-Options: DENY}} | clickjacking in older browsers (CSP frame-ancestors supersedes) |

### CSP rollout
1. Start with {{Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only}} and a report endpoint.
2. Inventory scripts, styles, connect targets; remove inline scripts or use **nonces** (generated per response) or hashes.
3. Tighten: {{default-src 'self'}}, explicit {{connect-src}} for APIs, {{script-src 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'}}, {{object-src 'none'}}, {{base-uri 'none'}}.
4. Enforce; keep reporting on; review violations.

### APIs
JSON APIs need fewer headers (HSTS, nosniff, no-store), but they matter for error pages and docs.
pts: HSTS, CSP, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP, no-store.
CSP frame-ancestors replaces X-Frame-Options.
Roll CSP out in report-only first.
Nonces or hashes, no unsafe-inline.
Keep violation reporting on.
questions.ex: A bank's CSP allowed unsafe-inline and a wildcard CDN; an XSS loaded a skimmer from that CDN. A nonce-based strict-dynamic CSP rolled out via report-only for three weeks blocked the same technique in a later test.

questions.q: Explain SSRF with a cloud example (metadata endpoint), and design defences for a feature that fetches URLs supplied by users (webhook targets, document imports).
questions.a:
### Mechanism
The server makes an HTTP request to a URL influenced by the attacker. Targets: cloud metadata ({{169.254.169.254}}) to steal instance credentials, internal admin services, localhost ports, or internal networks invisible from the internet. Redirects, DNS rebinding and alternative IP encodings ({{0x7f.1}}, IPv6-mapped) bypass naive checks.

### Defences
1. **Avoid** fetching arbitrary URLs where possible (upload files instead; allow-list partner domains).
2. **Allow-list** schemes ({{https}} only), hosts or domains, and ports.
3. **Resolve and validate IPs** at connection time (not just at validation time): block private, loopback, link-local, metadata, and internal ranges; re-validate after redirects or disable redirects.
4. **Network egress controls**: fetcher runs in an isolated network segment or via an egress proxy that enforces rules; no route to internal services or metadata.
5. **Cloud metadata hardening**: AWS IMDSv2 (session tokens, hop limit), Azure IMDS requires the {{Metadata: true}} header (which helps against simple SSRF, not all).
6. Timeouts, size limits, content-type checks on responses; never return raw responses to users.
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  A[Attacker submits URL] --> F[Fetch-preview feature]
  F --> V{Validate}
  V -->|resolve DNS, check IP against deny list| D1[Block private, loopback, link-local 169.254.x]
  V -->|scheme and port allow list| D2[Only https 443]
  V -->|ok| P[Egress proxy with allow list]
  P --> I[Internet target]
  F -.->|without controls| M[Cloud metadata endpoint, credentials leak]
pts: Server fetches attacker-influenced URLs.
Metadata endpoints and internal services are prime targets.
Allow-list schemes, hosts and ports.
Validate the IP at connect time; block redirects.
Isolate fetchers with egress controls; harden IMDS.
questions.ex: The 2019 Capital One breach used SSRF to reach the EC2 metadata service and steal role credentials. A bank's webhook feature later passed a pen test because fetches ran in an isolated subnet via an egress proxy with IP validation at connect time.

How does IMDSv2 help?
How do you safely support customer webhooks?
pit: Fetchers with access to internal networks.

questions.q: Why is insecure deserialization dangerous in .NET, which serializers and settings are risky, and how do you deserialize untrusted data safely?
questions.a:
### Danger
Deserializers that instantiate **types named in the payload** can be tricked into creating gadget objects whose constructors, setters or finalisers execute code (remote code execution), or into allocating huge graphs (DoS).

### Risky in .NET
| Serializer or setting | Risk |
|---|---|
| {{BinaryFormatter}}, {{SoapFormatter}}, {{NetDataContractSerializer}}, {{LosFormatter}}, {{ObjectStateFormatter}} | RCE; BinaryFormatter is removed in .NET 9 |
| Newtonsoft.Json with {{TypeNameHandling}} other than None | payload chooses types: RCE gadgets |
| {{XmlSerializer}} with types from input, {{DataContractSerializer}} with known types too broad | type confusion |
| YAML libraries constructing arbitrary types | same class |
| Polymorphic System.Text.Json with unchecked type discriminators | safe if discriminators map to an allow-list (the default design) |

### Safe practice
- Use **System.Text.Json** with concrete DTOs; for polymorphism use {{JsonDerivedType}} allow-lists.
- Never deserialize untrusted data into object or with type names.
- Limit depth and size ({{MaxDepth}}, request size limits).
- Validate after deserialization (DTO validation), then map to domain objects.
- Sign or encrypt data you round-trip through clients (view state, cookies) so it can't be tampered with.
pts: Type-controlled deserialization enables RCE gadgets.
BinaryFormatter family and TypeNameHandling are dangerous.
System.Text.Json with DTOs and discriminator allow-lists.
Limit depth and size; disallow unmapped members.
Sign round-tripped data.
questions.ex: A legacy WCF service accepted NetDataContractSerializer payloads from a partner network; a red team achieved code execution with a public gadget chain. Migrating the endpoint to System.Text.Json DTOs closed the path and removed an entire vulnerability class.

questions.q: Explain symmetric vs asymmetric encryption and authenticated encryption (AES-GCM). What are the most common cryptography mistakes in application code?
questions.a:
### Basics
- **Symmetric** (AES): one key, fast, for data at rest and bulk data.
- **Asymmetric** (RSA, ECC): key pairs, slow, for key exchange, signatures, encrypting small secrets to a public key.
- **Hybrid / envelope**: encrypt data with a random symmetric key, encrypt that key with an asymmetric or KMS key.
- **Authenticated encryption (AEAD)**: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 provide confidentiality **and** integrity; tampering is detected. Associated data (AAD) binds context (record id, tenant) without encrypting it.

### Common mistakes
| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| ECB mode | patterns leak |
| CBC without MAC, or MAC-then-encrypt errors | padding oracle attacks |
| **Nonce reuse with GCM** | catastrophic: keystream reuse and forgery |
| hard-coded keys, keys in config files | key compromise |
| rolling your own crypto or protocols | subtle breaks |
| using {{Random}} instead of {{RandomNumberGenerator}} | predictable values |
| comparing MACs with {{==}} | timing attacks; use fixed-time comparison |
| RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption | padding oracles; use OAEP |
| no key rotation or versioning | can't rotate after compromise |

### Rule
Use high-level, reviewed primitives (Data Protection API, Key Vault, libsodium-style APIs); store key version with ciphertext.
pts: Symmetric for bulk, asymmetric for exchange and signatures, envelope for both.
AEAD gives confidentiality and integrity; AAD binds context.
Never reuse GCM nonces; avoid ECB and unauthenticated CBC.
CSPRNG, fixed-time comparisons, OAEP.
Version keys for rotation; prefer high-level APIs.
questions.ex: A team encrypted card tokens with AES-CBC and a static IV, enabling an attacker with database access to detect equal values and tamper with ciphertexts. Moving to AES-GCM with random nonces, AAD per record and Key Vault-managed keys fixed both issues.

questions.q: Design webhook security for a payments provider sending you events: signatures, replay protection, key rotation, and what to do on verification failure.
questions.a:
### Signature options
| Option | How | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **HMAC-SHA256** with shared secret | provider signs {{timestamp + "." + body}}; you recompute and compare in fixed time | simple, common (Stripe-style) |
| **Asymmetric signature** (Ed25519, RSA-PSS, ECDSA) | provider signs with private key; you verify with published public key (JWKS) | no shared secret to leak on your side |
| **mTLS** | provider presents client certificate | transport-level, complements payload signatures |

### Replay protection
Include a **timestamp** in the signed content; reject if older than a tolerance (for example 5 minutes); record event ids and reject duplicates (also needed for idempotency).

### Rotation
Support **multiple active secrets or keys** (verify against any current key), with key ids in headers; rotate on a schedule and immediately on suspicion.

### Processing
Verify on the **raw body bytes** before parsing; respond 2xx quickly and process asynchronously (outbox or queue); idempotent handling by event id; failures return 4xx without leaking details; alert on spikes of signature failures (possible attack or misconfiguration).

### Don't
Trust IP allow-lists alone, verify after JSON re-serialisation, or log the secret.
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Payments provider
  participant W as Webhook endpoint
  participant Q as Queue
  P->>W: POST event with timestamp, event id, HMAC signature header
  W->>W: recompute HMAC over timestamp plus raw body with shared secret
  W->>W: constant-time compare, reject if timestamp older than 5 min
  W->>W: reject if event id already seen - replay guard
  W->>Q: enqueue verified event
  W-->>P: 200 quickly, process asynchronously
  Q->>Q: consumer fetches authoritative status from provider API before moving money
pts: HMAC or asymmetric signatures over timestamp and raw body.
Timestamp tolerance plus event-id dedupe against replay.
Multiple active keys for rotation.
Verify raw bytes before parsing; fixed-time comparison.
Acknowledge fast, process idempotently, alert on failures.
questions.ex: A merchant's webhook endpoint verified signatures after re-serialising JSON, so legitimate events failed intermittently and the team disabled verification "temporarily". An attacker later forged refund-completed events. Raw-body verification with a replay window fixed both problems.

questions.q: What does TLS actually guarantee, what are the common certificate validation mistakes in .NET code, and when do you use mTLS?
questions.a:
### Guarantees
Confidentiality and integrity in transit, and **server authentication** (the certificate chains to a trusted CA and matches the hostname). With mTLS, the client is authenticated too. TLS 1.3 (or 1.2 with modern cipher suites) with forward secrecy.

### Common mistakes
| Mistake | Effect |
|---|---|
| {{ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (...) => true}} | accepts any certificate: trivial man-in-the-middle |
| disabling hostname validation | any valid certificate for any domain works |
| pinning leaf certificates without rotation plan | outages on renewal |
| allowing TLS 1.0/1.1 or weak ciphers | downgrade and known attacks |
| ignoring revocation for high-value connections | compromised certificates accepted |
| private keys in source control or images | impersonation |

### mTLS use cases
Service-to-service (mesh or app-level), partner APIs and open banking (with certificate-bound tokens), connections to brokers and databases where supported.

### Operations
Automated issuance and renewal (cert-manager, Key Vault certificates), expiry monitoring, inventory of certificates and owners.
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  C->>S: ClientHello - supported versions, cipher suites, key share
  S->>C: ServerHello, key share, certificate chain, CertificateVerify, Finished
  C->>C: validate chain to trusted root, hostname, expiry, revocation
  C->>C: derive session keys from ECDHE shared secret
  C->>S: Finished
  Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 - one round trip, forward secrecy by default
  C->>S: encrypted application data
pts: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, server authentication.
Never accept any certificate; never skip hostname checks.
TLS 1.2+ with modern ciphers.
mTLS for services, partners, brokers.
Automate issuance, renewal and expiry monitoring.

questions.q: Design key management for encrypting sensitive data: KMS/HSM, envelope encryption, rotation, separation of duties and what happens on key compromise.
questions.a:
### Envelope encryption
- A **key encryption key (KEK)** lives in Azure Key Vault (Managed HSM for FIPS 140-3 level 3) or AWS KMS; it never leaves the HSM.
- Each record or file gets a random **data encryption key (DEK)**, used locally (AES-GCM).
- The DEK is **wrapped** (encrypted) by the KEK and stored next to the ciphertext with the KEK version.
- Decrypt: unwrap the DEK via KMS (authorised, logged), then decrypt locally. Cache unwrapped DEKs briefly for performance.

### Rotation
- KEK rotation: new version for new wraps; **rewrap** existing DEKs in the background (cheap: DEKs are small); data isn't re-encrypted.
- DEK rotation (re-encrypting data) only on compromise or policy.

### Separation of duties
Key administrators (create, rotate, set policy) differ from key users (applications with wrap/unwrap rights via managed identity); no one has both plus data access. Key operations logged to the SIEM.

### Compromise
Disable the compromised key version, rewrap with a new KEK, assess which data used it (key version metadata), re-encrypt if DEKs may be exposed, and investigate access logs.
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  APP[Application] -->|generate DEK| DEK[Random AES-256 DEK]
  DEK -->|encrypt data locally| CT[(Ciphertext + wrapped DEK + KEK version)]
  APP -->|wrap DEK| KV[Key Vault HSM - KEK never leaves]
  KV -->|wrapped DEK| CT
  APP -->|unwrap on read, logged| KV
pts: KEK in HSM-backed KMS; per-record DEKs.
Store wrapped DEK and KEK version with ciphertext.
Rotate KEKs by rewrapping DEKs.
Separate key admins from key users.
Compromise plan: disable, rewrap, assess by version.
questions.ex: An insurer stored a single AES key in app settings for all documents; when a contractor's laptop was compromised, all documents had to be treated as exposed. The redesign with envelope encryption, Key Vault HSM and per-document DEKs made future exposure analysis possible per key version.

questions.q: How should applications authenticate to databases, queues and APIs without secrets? Where are secrets still unavoidable and how are they protected?
questions.a:
### Prefer identity over secrets
- **Managed identities** (Azure) or IAM roles (AWS) or workload identity federation (Kubernetes service accounts to cloud identities).
- Azure SQL, Storage, Service Bus, Event Hubs, Key Vault, Cosmos DB all accept Entra ID tokens: no connection-string passwords.
- Service-to-service: OAuth client credentials with **private_key_jwt** or certificate credentials, or mesh mTLS identities.

### Still unavoidable
Third-party API keys, legacy databases with SQL auth, partner shared secrets (webhooks), on-premise systems.

### Protecting them
- Store in Key Vault or Secrets Manager; the app reads them via its identity at runtime; cache with refresh.
- Never in source, images, environment variables in manifests committed to Git, or logs.
- Rotation automated where possible (dual secrets during rollover); short-lived credentials where possible (Vault dynamic database credentials).
- Secret scanning with push protection in repositories; alerts on usage anomalies.
- Inventory: which secret, which owner, which consumers, rotation date.
pts: Managed identities and workload federation over secrets.
Entra ID auth for SQL, Storage, Service Bus, Key Vault.
Remaining secrets in Key Vault, read at runtime.
Automated rotation and dynamic credentials.
Secret scanning and an owned inventory.
questions.ex: A leaked connection string with a SQL admin password in a public GitHub gist led to a data breach investigation. Moving 40 services to managed identity with Entra ID authentication removed all database passwords; the remaining 6 third-party keys were vaulted with 90-day rotation.

questions.q: Run a STRIDE threat model for a new "pay a new payee" feature. What do you produce and how do you keep threat modelling lightweight?
questions.a:
### Scope and diagram
Data flow: mobile app, API gateway, payments API, payee service, fraud scoring, ledger, notification service, external scheme. Trust boundaries: internet to gateway, gateway to services, services to third parties.

### STRIDE per element
| Threat | Example | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Spoofing** | stolen session adds payee | step-up authentication (SCA) for new payees, device binding |
| **Tampering** | changing payee account in transit or in API calls | TLS, server-side validation, signed confirmation of payee details |
| **Repudiation** | customer denies adding payee | audit events with device, IP, authentication method |
| **Information disclosure** | payee name lookup reveals account holder names (enumeration) | confirmation-of-payee returns match levels, rate limited |
| **Denial of service** | bots adding payees to probe accounts | rate limits per customer and device, CAPTCHA on anomalies |
| **Elevation of privilege** | BOLA adding payee to another customer's account | resource-based authorisation, tests |
Plus abuse cases: authorised push payment fraud (social engineering) needs cooling-off periods, warnings, and fraud scoring.

### Output
Diagram, threat list with risk rating, mitigations mapped to backlog items and tests, residual risks accepted by an owner.

### Lightweight
30 to 60 minutes at design time with engineers, product and security champion; revisit on significant change; templates per architecture pattern.

questions.q: Compare SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, secret scanning and fuzzing. Where does each run in the delivery pipeline and what does each miss?
questions.a:
| Technique | How | Where | Finds | Misses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SAST** (CodeQL, Roslyn analyzers, Semgrep) | analyses source code | IDE, PR | injection patterns, unsafe APIs, crypto misuse | runtime config, business logic, many false positives |
| **SCA** (Dependabot, Snyk, dotnet list package --vulnerable) | inventories dependencies against CVE databases | PR, nightly, registry | known vulnerable libraries, licences | unknown vulnerabilities, reachability (unless supported) |
| **Secret scanning** | pattern detection in commits | push (with push protection), PR | leaked keys and tokens | secrets in non-standard formats |
| **DAST** (OWASP ZAP, Burp) | attacks a running app | staging, nightly | misconfigurations, headers, some injection, auth flaws | code paths not reached, business logic |
| **IAST** | agent inside the running app during tests | integration test runs | precise data-flow findings with low false positives | only exercised paths; runtime support |
| **Fuzzing** (SharpFuzz, API fuzzers like RESTler) | malformed or random inputs | nightly for parsers and APIs | crashes, DoS, parser bugs | logic flaws |
| **Pen testing and bug bounty** | humans | periodic, pre-launch | business logic, chained issues, BOLA | depends on scope and skill |

### Programme
Fast checks blocking PRs (SAST high-confidence rules, SCA criticals, secrets), slower scans non-blocking with triage SLAs, human testing for high-risk features. Track findings to closure; tune rules to keep false positives low or developers will ignore them.

questions.q: What is the difference between input validation and output encoding, and how do you handle file uploads (statements, ID documents) securely?
questions.a:
### Validation vs encoding
- **Input validation**: reject data that doesn't fit the expected shape (type, length, format, range, allow-listed values) at the boundary. Reduces attack surface and garbage, but cannot make data "safe" for every context.
- **Output encoding**: encode data for the context where it is used (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL, SQL parameters, shell). This is what actually prevents injection.
Do both: validate early, encode late.

### File uploads
| Control | Why |
|---|---|
| Size limits per route | DoS, storage abuse |
| Allow-listed types, verified by **content** (magic bytes), not extension or Content-Type header | disguised executables |
| Generate server-side file names; never use user file names in paths | path traversal |
| Store outside the web root, in private blob storage | direct execution or access |
| **Malware scanning** before use (Defender for Storage, ClamAV) | malware |
| Re-encode images, strip metadata (EXIF with GPS) | embedded payloads, privacy |
| PDF handling: sanitise or render in sandboxed services | malicious PDFs |
| Download with {{Content-Disposition: attachment}} and correct content type | XSS via uploaded HTML or SVG |
| Access via authorised, short-lived signed URLs | data leaks |
pts: Validate at the boundary; encode for the output context.
Uploads: size limits, content-based type checks.
Server-generated names, private storage.
Malware scanning before use; re-encode images.
Serve as attachments via signed URLs.
questions.ex: An onboarding flow accepted SVG "ID documents" and displayed them inline in a back-office tool; an embedded script ran in staff browsers. Allow-listing PDF, JPEG and PNG by magic bytes and serving files as attachments closed it.

questions.q: Which security events should applications emit, and how do they become detections in a SIEM?
questions.a:
### Application security events
| Event | Detection use |
|---|---|
| authentication success and failure, MFA challenges, lockouts | credential stuffing, account takeover |
| authorisation denials (403, BOLA attempts returning 404 for other users' ids) | probing and enumeration |
| privilege changes, role grants, admin actions | insider abuse, compromise |
| sensitive data access and exports (bulk downloads) | exfiltration |
| security control changes (MFA disabled, payee added, limit raised, contact details changed) | account takeover patterns |
| input validation spikes, WAF blocks | attacks in progress |
| token anomalies (reuse of refresh tokens, impossible travel) | session theft |

### Event quality
Structured, consistent schema (who, what, when, where, outcome, reason), reliable delivery (not sampled), synchronised time, no secrets or excessive PII.

### Detections
SIEM rules (Microsoft Sentinel KQL, Splunk SPL) correlating events: many failed logins across accounts from one IP range; contact details change followed by new payee and large payment within an hour; bulk exports outside working hours. Detections are versioned, tested with sample data, and tuned; each has a response playbook (SOAR).

### Keeping PII and secrets out of logs
Logs are copied widely (log platform, SIEM, support tools, vendors), so a card number in a log line becomes a PCI scope problem everywhere it lands.
- **Classify fields** in DTOs ([PersonalData], [Sensitive]) and redact them in the logging pipeline, not by developer discipline.
- **Log identifiers, not values**: customer id and a masked account ("****1234"), never full PAN, CVV, passwords, tokens or full request bodies.
- **Scan logs** for patterns (PAN with Luhn check, IBAN, JWTs) and alert on hits; treat a hit as an incident.
- **Separate retention**: security audit logs kept long and tamper-evident; debug logs short.

~~~csharp
// Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction: redact classified data automatically in structured logs
builder.Services.AddRedaction(r =>
{
    r.SetRedactor<ErasingRedactor>(new DataClassificationSet(BankTaxonomy.Secret));
    r.SetRedactor<StarRedactor>(new DataClassificationSet(BankTaxonomy.Personal));
});
builder.Logging.EnableRedaction();

public partial class TransferLog
{
    [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Transfer created for {CustomerId} to {Iban}")]
    public static partial void Created(ILogger logger, string customerId, [PersonalData] string iban);
}
~~~
pts: Emit authn, authz denials, privilege, data access, control changes.
Structured, reliable, time-synced, no secrets.
SIEM correlates events into detections.
Detections versioned, tested, tuned.
Each detection has a playbook.

questions.q: A critical zero-day in a widely used library (think Log4Shell) is announced at 6 p.m. Walk through your response for the next 72 hours.
questions.a:
### Hour 0 to 2: assess
- Read the advisory: affected versions, exploit preconditions, active exploitation (CISA KEV), available fixes or mitigations.
- **Find exposure** fast: SBOMs and SCA inventory across repos, images in registries and **running** workloads (runtime scanners), vendor products (ask vendors), transitive dependencies.
- Declare a security incident with an incident commander; open a tracking board.

### Hour 2 to 12: mitigate
- **Edge mitigations**: WAF rules for exploit patterns, egress blocks (for Log4Shell: outbound LDAP and JNDI), configuration flags that disable the vulnerable feature.
- Prioritise internet-facing and high-value systems.
- Patch or upgrade where a fix exists; rebuild images (base image updates too).
- Hunt for exploitation: logs, WAF hits, outbound connections, new processes since disclosure (or earlier if exploited before disclosure).

### Hour 12 to 72: remediate and verify
- Roll out fixes through normal pipelines with expedited approval; track per service to 100%.
- Verify with scanners and runtime inventory; confirm no vulnerable versions remain in registries.
- Communicate to leadership, customers if needed, regulators if criteria met.
- Post-incident: improve inventory speed, dependency hygiene, egress controls.

questions.q: Design a vulnerability management programme that teams actually follow. How do you prioritise thousands of findings?
questions.a:
### Problem
CVSS alone marks thousands of findings "high"; teams drown and fix nothing.

### Risk-based prioritisation
| Factor | Source |
|---|---|
| Severity | CVSS base score |
| **Exploitation in the wild** | CISA KEV catalogue |
| **Likelihood of exploitation** | EPSS probability |
| Reachability | is the vulnerable function used? (SCA reachability, runtime loaded libraries) |
| Exposure | internet-facing, internal, offline batch |
| Asset criticality | tier-1 payments vs internal tool, data sensitivity |
| Compensating controls | WAF, network isolation |

### SLAs by computed priority
For example P1 (KEV or EPSS high, internet-facing, critical asset): 72 hours; P2: 14 days; P3: 60 days; P4: next routine update.

### Programme mechanics
- One deduplicated backlog per team (from SCA, container scans, SAST, pen tests), integrated into their normal work tracker.
- Automated fixes where possible (Renovate, base image rebuilds).
- Exceptions with expiry and risk acceptance by an owner.
- Metrics: SLA compliance by priority, mean time to remediate, open P1s, age distribution; reported to leadership.
pts: CVSS alone overwhelms teams.
Prioritise with KEV, EPSS, reachability, exposure, criticality.
SLAs per computed priority.
Single deduplicated backlog per team; automation for fixes.
Exceptions with expiry; metrics to leadership.
questions.ex: A bank had 38,000 open "high" findings and a 4% monthly fix rate. Risk-based prioritisation reduced the actionable P1 and P2 set to 410; with automated base image rebuilds and Renovate, SLA compliance reached 92% within two quarters.

Who approves exceptions?
How do you handle vendor appliances?
pit: Findings in a separate tool teams never open.

questions.q: What does zero trust mean concretely for a bank's applications, and how do you move from a perimeter model incrementally?
questions.a:
### Principles (NIST SP 800-207 in practice)
- No implicit trust from network location: every request is authenticated and authorised.
- Strong identity for users (phishing-resistant MFA, device health) and workloads (managed identities, mTLS, SPIFFE).
- Least privilege per request, continuously evaluated (short-lived tokens, risk signals).
- Assume breach: segment, monitor, limit blast radius.

### Concrete controls
| Area | Control |
|---|---|
| Users | SSO with conditional access (device compliance, location, risk), phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) for staff, just-in-time admin |
| Workloads | managed identity everywhere, mTLS service-to-service, token audiences per service |
| Network | micro-segmentation (NetworkPolicies, private endpoints), no flat VPN access to everything |
| Data | encryption, classification, access logged |
| Admin access | privileged access workstations, PAM, session recording, no standing access |
| Monitoring | identity and access analytics, anomaly detection |

### Incremental path
1. Identity foundation (SSO everywhere, MFA, inventory of apps and service accounts).
2. Replace VPN-to-everything with identity-aware proxies for internal apps.
3. Managed identities and remove secrets.
4. Segment critical systems (payments, CDE) first.
5. Service-level authorisation (mesh or app) and default deny.
6. Continuous verification and metrics (coverage of MFA, workloads with identity, segments enforced).

questions.q: A B2B SaaS banking platform stores many corporate clients in shared databases. How do you guarantee tenant isolation in code and in the database?
questions.a:
### Isolation models
| Model | Isolation | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| database per tenant | strong; per-tenant keys and backups | highest ops cost |
| schema per tenant | medium | migrations multiply |
| shared tables with tenant column | weakest by default | cheapest |
Large or regulated tenants often get dedicated databases; the long tail shares.

### Shared-table controls (defence in depth)
1. **Tenant resolution** from the authenticated token (never from a header or path alone).
2. **EF Core global query filters** on every tenant-owned entity, plus a guard that inserts set TenantId.
3. **Database row-level security** (SQL Server security policies, PostgreSQL RLS) using {{SESSION_CONTEXT}} or a session variable set per connection: even a forgotten filter or raw SQL can't cross tenants.
4. **Per-tenant encryption keys** for sensitive columns (crypto isolation and tenant offboarding).
5. Tests: cross-tenant access tests in CI for every endpoint; chaos tests running queries without filters to prove RLS blocks them.
6. Telemetry and caches keyed by tenant.
pts: Choose isolation model by tenant size and regulation.
Resolve tenant from the token.
EF global filters plus database RLS.
Per-tenant encryption keys.
Cross-tenant tests and tenant-keyed caches.
questions.ex: A reporting query written with Dapper forgot the tenant filter and showed one corporate client another's payments for an hour. After adding SQL Server RLS with read-only session context, the same mistake in a later raw query returned no rows instead of leaking.

questions.q: Design a secure payment initiation API for corporate clients. Which controls protect against fraud, tampering, replay and abuse?
questions.a:
### Authentication and authorisation
- OAuth client credentials with **private_key_jwt** or **mTLS** (certificate-bound tokens); scopes per operation.
- User-level approval for corporate payments (maker-checker): the initiating system and an approving user with step-up authentication.
- Object-level checks: the client may debit only its own accounts.

### Integrity and replay
- **Request signing** (for example JWS detached signature over the body, or HTTP Message Signatures RFC 9421) so payment details can't be altered by intermediaries.
- **Idempotency-Key** required; duplicates return the original result.
- Timestamps and nonces in signed content; short validity.

### Business controls
- Per-client limits (per payment, daily, per beneficiary country), velocity checks, new-beneficiary cooling periods.
- Sanctions screening, fraud scoring, confirmation of payee.
- Cut-off time enforcement and duplicate detection (same amount and beneficiary within a window).

### Abuse and availability
Rate limits per client, request size limits, schema validation, strict TLS.

### Audit and monitoring
Signed request stored for non-repudiation, audit events, detection rules for unusual patterns, webhooks signed for status updates.

questions.q: Compare TDE, Always Encrypted, application-level field encryption and tokenisation for protecting sensitive banking data. What threat does each actually address?
questions.a:
| Technique | Protects against | Doesn't protect against | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TDE / storage encryption** | stolen disks, backups, files | anyone with database access (DBAs, compromised app, SQL injection) | transparent, no app changes |
| **Always Encrypted** (SQL Server) | DBAs and cloud operators seeing plaintext; keys held client-side | the application (it decrypts) | limited querying (deterministic equality only, or secure enclaves), driver support |
| **App-level field encryption** (AES-GCM with KMS) | DB-level access, backups, many insiders | compromised application | you build key management and querying limits |
| **Tokenisation** | systems handling tokens never see real data (shrinks PCI scope) | token vault compromise | a vault service to operate or buy; format-preserving tokens possible |
| **Hashing (keyed)** for lookups | lookup without storing plaintext (e.g., national id search) | brute force if unkeyed | HMAC with secret key needed |

### Choosing for a bank
- Card numbers: tokenisation via a PCI-certified vault; most systems store tokens only.
- National ids, account numbers needing equality lookup: Always Encrypted deterministic or HMAC index plus randomised encryption for the value.
- Documents: envelope encryption in storage with per-document keys.
- Everything: TDE and storage encryption as the baseline.

### Key point
Ask "who can see plaintext?": each technique moves that boundary.
pts: TDE protects media, not database users.
Always Encrypted hides data from DBAs, not the app.
App-level encryption with KMS for field protection.
Tokenisation shrinks PCI scope.
Ask who can see plaintext.
questions.ex: A bank believed TDE protected customer national ids; an auditor pointed out that 40 DBAs and every reporting tool could read them. Moving to HMAC lookup keys plus randomised field encryption reduced plaintext access to the onboarding service and a break-glass procedure.

questions.q: Explain mass assignment and broken object property level authorisation with examples in ASP.NET Core and EF Core, and how to prevent them systematically.
questions.a:
### Mass assignment (write side)
The API binds request JSON directly onto an entity, so clients can set fields they shouldn't: {{"isVerified": true}}, {{"creditLimit": 50000}}, {{"ownerId": "..."}}, {{"status": "Approved"}}.

### Excessive data exposure (read side)
Returning entities serialises everything: internal flags, risk scores, other users' data via navigation properties.

### Prevention
1. **Separate request and response DTOs** per operation; never bind to entities.
2. Map explicitly (manual mapping or source-generated mappers with explicit configuration).
3. For PATCH, allow-list patchable properties per role; validate each operation.
4. Serialiser settings: reject unknown properties ({{UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow}}) to surface attempts.
5. Property-level authorisation where roles differ (support can see masked fields; customer sees own).
6. Tests asserting that forbidden properties are ignored or rejected; contract snapshots of responses to catch accidental new fields.
pts: Binding to entities lets clients set protected fields.
Returning entities leaks internal fields.
Operation-specific request and response DTOs.
Reject unknown properties; allow-list PATCH fields.
Property-level authz and response contract tests.
questions.ex: A loan application API bound JSON directly to the LoanApplication entity; a tester set "approvedAmount" in the request and it persisted. Moving to DTOs and adding UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow made such attempts fail loudly and visible in security monitoring.

questions.q: Attackers fire 50 parallel withdrawal requests and overdraw an account; others redeem a single-use voucher 20 times. Explain the race and fix it properly.
questions.a:
### The flaw: check-then-act (TOCTOU)
Each request reads the balance (100), checks amount (80) is affordable, then writes. In parallel, all reads happen before any write, so all pass. Same for "voucher not yet redeemed" checks.

### Fixes
| Fix | How |
|---|---|
| **Atomic conditional update** | {{UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - @amt WHERE Id = @id AND Balance >= @amt}}; check rows affected |
| **Optimistic concurrency** | rowversion or version column; concurrent writes fail and retry with fresh state |
| **Pessimistic locking** | {{SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK)}} within a transaction for the decision window |
| **Unique constraints** | voucher redemption table with unique voucher id: second insert fails |
| **Single writer per account** | serialise commands per aggregate (actor, partitioned queue) |
| **Idempotency keys** | stop client-retry duplicates (not malicious parallel distinct requests) |

### Testing
Concurrency tests firing parallel requests in CI against a real database; business logic abuse cases in threat models; monitoring for limit breaches (negative balances, multiple redemptions) as detections.
pts: Check-then-act races allow parallel abuse.
Atomic conditional updates enforce invariants.
Optimistic or pessimistic concurrency where needed.
Unique constraints for single-use resources.
Test with parallel requests; detect breaches.

questions.q: Harden containers and Kubernetes workloads for a payments platform. What are the highest-value controls?
questions.a:
### Image
Minimal base images (chiselled or distroless .NET images), non-root user, no shells or package managers in runtime images, pinned digests, scanned and signed, rebuilt regularly for patches.

### Pod
| Control | Setting |

| run as non-root | {{runAsNonRoot: true}}, explicit UID |

questions.q: Most cloud breaches come from misconfiguration. How do you prevent and detect misconfigurations across hundreds of subscriptions or accounts?
questions.a:
### Prevent (guardrails)
- **Landing zones** with management groups or organisational units, baseline policies inherited by all subscriptions.
- **Azure Policy / AWS SCPs and Config rules** denying: public storage, public IPs on databases, unencrypted resources, disallowed regions (residency), missing diagnostic settings, key vaults without purge protection.
- **Infrastructure as code** with policy checks in PRs (Checkov, conftest) so issues fail before deployment.
- Private endpoints by default; no public network access for data services.

### Detect

- Drift detection between IaC and actual state.
- Identity analysis: over-privileged roles, unused permissions, external access.

### Respond
Findings routed to owning teams with SLAs; auto-remediation for safe cases (enable encryption, block public access); exceptions with expiry.

### Ownership
Tagging (owner, data classification, cost centre) enforced by policy so every finding has a team.

questions.q: Explain dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks against NuGet and npm, and how you configure feeds and builds to prevent them.
questions.a:
### Attacks
- **Dependency confusion**: an internal package name ({{Bank.Payments.Contracts}}) is published by an attacker to the public registry with a higher version; misconfigured builds resolve the public one.
- **Typosquatting**: {{Newtonsoft.Jsonn}}, {{reqeusts}}; developers install the wrong package.
- **Compromised maintainers or packages**: legitimate packages updated with malicious code (install scripts in npm).
- **Malicious install scripts**: npm {{postinstall}} runs code on developer machines and CI.

### Prevention
| Control | How |
|---|---|
| Single upstream-proxying private feed | Azure Artifacts or Artifactory as the only source; it proxies nuget.org and npmjs with caching |
| **NuGet package source mapping** | internal prefixes ({{Bank.*}}) can only come from the internal feed |
| Reserve prefixes on nuget.org and npm scopes ({{@bank}}) | attackers can't publish your names |
| Lock files and locked restores | no surprise resolutions |
| npm {{--ignore-scripts}} in CI where possible, allow-list packages needing scripts | install-time code execution |
| Minimum release age, review of new dependencies (dependency review in PRs) | fresh malicious releases |
| SBOMs and provenance checks | inventory and trust |

  <packageSources>
    <clear />
    <add key="bank-internal" value="https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/bank/_packaging/internal/nuget/v3/index.json" />
    <add key="bank-upstream" value="https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/bank/_packaging/public-proxy/nuget/v3/index.json" />
  </packageSources>
  <packageSourceMapping>
    <packageSource key="bank-internal">
      <package pattern="Bank.*" />
    </packageSource>
    <packageSource key="bank-upstream">
      <package pattern="*" />
    </packageSource>
  </packageSourceMapping>
</configuration>
<!-- .npmrc: @bank:registry=https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/bank/_packaging/internal/npm/registry/  and  ignore-scripts=true -->
~~~
pts: Dependency confusion abuses resolution across feeds.
Typosquatting and compromised packages.
Single proxied feed plus package source mapping.
Reserve prefixes and scopes publicly.
Lock files, ignore install scripts, review new dependencies.

questions.q: Secure an Angular or React banking SPA: token handling, third-party scripts (Magecart-style skimming), dependency risks and CSP.
questions.a:
### Tokens
- Prefer a **BFF** with HttpOnly SameSite cookies (tokens never reach JavaScript).
- If tokens must live in the browser: in memory only (not localStorage), short-lived access tokens, refresh token rotation with reuse detection, DPoP binding where supported.

### Third-party scripts
Every analytics, chat or tag-manager script runs with full access to the page (form fields, card inputs). Controls:
- Minimise third parties on sensitive pages (login, payments); none on card entry pages (use the PSP's hosted fields in an iframe).
- **Subresource Integrity** ({{integrity}} attribute) for scripts loaded from CDNs.
- Strict **CSP** ({{script-src}} with nonces, {{connect-src}} allow-list blocks exfiltration to unknown domains).
- Monitor for script changes (PCI DSS 4.0 requires inventory and integrity monitoring of payment page scripts).

### Dependencies
npm supply chain: lock files, review new packages, minimum release age, SCA, ignore install scripts in CI.

### Other
Avoid secrets in the bundle (all client code is public), validate everything server-side, protect against clickjacking, and use framework sanitisation (no bypasses).

questions.q: Design customer authentication for a digital bank: MFA options, phishing resistance, step-up for risky actions, and secure account recovery.
questions.a:
### Factor strength
| Factor | Phishing resistant | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SMS OTP | no; SIM swap risk | fallback only |
| TOTP app | no (real-time phishing proxies) | better than SMS |
| Push approval | partly (number matching helps); push fatigue attacks | common in apps |
| **Passkeys / FIDO2 / WebAuthn** | **yes**: origin-bound keys | best for web and mobile |
| Device binding in mobile app (key in secure enclave, biometric unlock) | yes, if bound to the app and device | standard for banking apps |

### Step-up (dynamic linking)
PSD2 SCA: high-risk actions (new payee, large payment, changing contact details) require fresh strong authentication **bound to the transaction details** (amount and payee shown and signed), so a stolen session can't approve something else.

### Risk-based authentication
Device reputation, behavioural signals, geolocation anomalies, velocity; challenge more when risk is high.

### Account recovery (the weakest link)
- Don't let recovery bypass MFA via email-only reset.
- Require identity proofing (document plus liveness) or existing bound device; cooling-off periods for new devices and sensitive changes; notify all channels on changes.
- Help desk scripts resistant to social engineering; no agent-only overrides without second approval.

  S --> A{Risky action? new payee, large payment}
  A -->|yes| SU[Step-up: transaction signing showing payee and amount]
  A -->|no| OK[Proceed]
  SU --> OK
  C --> S

questions.q: Security and fraud teams both deal with account takeover. How do you design ATO detection and response, and where do security and fraud responsibilities split?
questions.a:
### ATO kill chain
Credential stuffing or phishing, then login, then changes to contact details or devices, then new payees or limits, then cash-out. Each step leaves signals.

### Detection signals
| Stage | Signals |
|---|---|
| login | failed attempts across many accounts from IP ranges, breached credentials, unusual device or location, bot signals |
| session | new device enrolment, impossible travel, session anomalies |
| changes | contact detail changes, MFA reset, new device binding |
| transactions | new payee plus large payment, unusual time, mule-account destinations |

### Response
- Real-time risk scoring at each step: allow, challenge (step-up), hold (delay payment for review), block.
- Automatic holds on payments after recent sensitive changes (cooling-off).
- Customer notifications on every sensitive change through existing channels.
- Fast case management for analysts; reversal or recall of payments where possible.

### Split
- **Security**: authentication systems, credential stuffing defences, bot management, session security, infrastructure compromise.
- **Fraud**: transaction risk, mule detection, customer-level behaviour, recovery of funds.
- **Shared**: event pipeline and signals, joint detection rules, a single customer risk view.
pts: ATO follows a chain: login, changes, payees, cash-out.
Signals at each stage.
Allow, step-up, hold or block in real time.
Cooling-off after sensitive changes; notify customers.
Security owns auth and bots; fraud owns transactions; share signals.
questions.ex: A bank's security team blocked bots at login while fraud scored payments separately; attackers who passed login changed phone numbers and paid out within 20 minutes. Sharing signals so a recent phone change raised payment risk, plus a 24-hour hold for new payees, cut ATO losses by 70%.

questions.q: What should a security-focused code review look for in a .NET and Angular pull request, and how do you scale it beyond the security team?
questions.a:
### Checklist (high-value items)
| Area | Look for |
|---|---|
| Authorisation | every endpoint has a policy; object-level checks for ids; no trust in client-supplied ids or roles |
| Input and data binding | DTOs, not entities; validation; no raw SQL concatenation; safe deserialisation |
| Output | no bypassSecurityTrust or dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data; correct content types |
| Secrets and config | no secrets in code; no accept-all certificate validators; secure defaults |
| Crypto | standard primitives, no custom crypto, RandomNumberGenerator, fixed-time comparisons |
| Logging | no secrets or PII; security events emitted for sensitive actions |
| Concurrency and business logic | check-then-act on balances, limits, single-use items |
| External calls | SSRF on user-supplied URLs, timeouts, TLS validation |
| Dependencies | new packages justified, maintained, licensed |
| Errors | no stack traces or internal details to clients |

### Scaling
- **Automate** what can be automated (CodeQL, analyzers, Semgrep rules for internal patterns) so humans focus on logic.
- **Security champions** in each team review high-risk changes; CODEOWNERS routes security-sensitive paths (auth, crypto, payments) to champions.
- PR templates with a short security section ("does this change auth, data exposure, external calls?").
- Security team reviews only flagged high-risk changes and does periodic sampling.

  - metavariable-regex: { metavariable: $ENTITY, regex: "^(Customer|Account|Payment|LoanApplication)$" }
~~~

questions.q: How do you get value from penetration tests, red teaming and bug bounties rather than a yearly PDF? Scope, timing, triage and fixing.
questions.a:
### Choose the right exercise
| Exercise | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Penetration test** | find vulnerabilities in a defined scope (app, API, infrastructure), often pre-launch or annually for compliance |
| **Red team** | test detection and response against a realistic adversary with objectives (reach payment systems) |
| **Purple team** | red and blue working together to improve detections |
| **Bug bounty** | continuous testing by external researchers; pay for valid findings |
| Regulatory threat-led testing (TIBER-EU, CBEST, DORA TLPT) | intelligence-led red teaming of critical functions |

### Getting value
- Scope by **risk** (new payment flows, auth changes) and timing it **before** launch with time to fix.
- Provide documentation, test accounts and architecture context (grey box) for depth.
- Findings go into team backlogs with severity-based SLAs, with retesting.
- Root-cause analysis: classes of bugs fed back into automated checks (a BOLA finding becomes a test pattern for all endpoints).
- Bug bounty: clear scope and safe harbour, fast triage (days), fair payouts, duplicates handling.

### Metrics
Time to fix by severity, recurrence of bug classes, detection rate in red team exercises.

questions.q: How do you prevent and detect bulk data exfiltration from banking systems, whether by an attacker with stolen credentials or a malicious insider?
questions.a:
### Prevent
- **Least privilege and need-to-know**: support staff see masked data; bulk export capabilities restricted to few roles with approval.
- **Query limits** in applications (page sizes, export row limits, rate limits per user).
- **No direct production database access** for humans; break-glass with approval and session recording.
- **Egress controls**: no internet from data environments; approved transfer channels only; DLP on email and endpoints.
- **Data minimisation**: don't replicate production data to lower environments (use synthetic or masked data).

### Detect
| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| unusual volume per user or service | 10x normal record reads |
| off-hours bulk access | exports at 3 a.m. |
| access to many unrelated customers | support agent viewing 500 profiles |
| new egress destinations | data service calling unknown hosts |
| database audit | large SELECTs from service accounts outside known patterns |
User and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) baselines per role.

### Respond
Automatic session termination or step-up on anomalies, investigation playbooks, legal and HR involvement for insiders.
pts: Least privilege, masking, restricted exports.
Query and rate limits in applications.
No direct human DB access; egress controls.
UEBA baselines detect unusual access.
Automated response and playbooks.

questions.q: Explain application-level denial of service: ReDoS, zip bombs, XML bombs, expensive queries and unbounded allocations. How do you defend in .NET?
questions.a:
### Attacks
| Attack | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **ReDoS** | regex with nested quantifiers ({{(a+)+$}}) backtracks exponentially on crafted input |
| **Zip bomb** | tiny archive expanding to gigabytes |
| **XML bomb** (billion laughs) | entity expansion |
| **Expensive queries** | unbounded page sizes, wildcard searches, deep GraphQL queries |
| **Large payloads** | huge JSON bodies or deep nesting |
| **Hash flooding** | crafted keys colliding (mitigated in .NET by randomised string hashing) |
| **Slow requests** | slowloris, slow body uploads |

### .NET defences
- Regex: timeouts ({{matchTimeout}}), {{RegexOptions.NonBacktracking}} (.NET 7+) for user-influenced patterns or inputs, source-generated regexes reviewed.
- Archives: check entry counts, total uncompressed size and ratios while streaming; refuse nested archives.
- XML: {{DtdProcessing.Prohibit}} (default for XmlReader in modern .NET); limit sizes.
- JSON: request body limits (Kestrel MaxRequestBodySize), {{MaxDepth}}.
- Queries: enforce max page size, require filters for search, query cost limits (GraphQL), timeouts and cancellation tokens.
- Kestrel limits: header sizes, min data rates; rate limiting and concurrency limits per client.

### Volumetric and protocol DDoS (beyond application-level DoS)
| Layer | Attack | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Network L3 and L4 | UDP floods, SYN floods, reflection and amplification | cloud provider or scrubbing-centre DDoS protection, anycast absorption |
| TLS | handshake exhaustion | edge termination at a CDN or front door with large capacity |
| HTTP L7 | request floods that look legitimate, credential stuffing | WAF rate rules, bot management, challenge pages, per-client quotas |
| Application | expensive endpoints (search, PDF generation, login) | per-user and per-endpoint limits, queue heavy work, cache, timeouts |

Design rules:
- Never expose origin servers directly; only accept traffic from the edge (private origin or IP allow list plus a shared secret header).
- Rate limit by authenticated identity first, IP second (carrier NAT puts many customers behind one IP).
- Have a runbook: who enables "under attack" mode, which features degrade first (statements export before payments), and how you talk to customers.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Internet traffic] --> E[Edge: anycast CDN, DDoS scrubbing]
  E --> W[WAF: rate rules, bot detection]
  W --> G[API gateway: per-client quotas]
  G --> S[Services: timeouts, bulkheads, load shedding]
  O[Origin] -.->|only accepts edge traffic| E
~~~

~~~csharp
// ASP.NET Core rate limiting: partition by authenticated customer, fall back to IP
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(o =>
{
    o.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
    o.AddPolicy("per-customer", ctx =>
    {
        string key = ctx.User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value ?? ctx.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "anon";
        return RateLimitPartition.GetTokenBucketLimiter(key, _ => new TokenBucketRateLimiterOptions
        {
            TokenLimit = 20, TokensPerPeriod = 10, ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), QueueLimit = 0
        });
    });
});
~~~
pts: ReDoS, zip and XML bombs, expensive queries, large payloads, slow requests.
NonBacktracking regex and timeouts.
Stream archives with ratio, size and count limits.
DTD prohibited; JSON depth and size limits.
Page-size caps, cost limits, Kestrel limits, rate limiting.

questions.q: Establish a secure SDLC across 60 engineering teams. What are the phases, controls, and how do you avoid it becoming a bureaucratic gate?
questions.a:
### Phases and controls
| Phase | Controls |
|---|---|
| Requirements | security and privacy requirements from templates (ASVS levels per data class); abuse cases |
| Design | lightweight threat modelling for significant changes; security architecture patterns (approved reference designs) |
| Build | secure defaults in templates; IDE and PR checks (SAST, SCA, secrets); security champions reviews |
| Test | DAST, API fuzzing, security unit tests (BOLA, authz), pen tests for high-risk launches |
| Release | signed artifacts, provenance, policy gates, production readiness |
| Operate | monitoring and detections, vulnerability SLAs, incident response, bug bounty |

### Avoiding bureaucracy
- **Risk tiers**: tier-1 (payments, auth, PII) get deeper reviews; tier-3 internal tools mostly automated checks.
- **Paved roads**: if teams use the golden path (templates, pipelines, auth libraries), most controls are already satisfied.
- **Automate evidence** instead of documents.
- Security champions embedded, not a central queue.
- Measure flow (time added by security activities) as well as outcomes.

### Governance
OWASP SAMM for maturity assessment, metrics to leadership, policies mapped to frameworks (ISO 27001, PCI, DORA), exceptions with expiry.

|---|---|---|
| **PCI DSS 4.0** | cardholder data | scope reduction (tokenisation), segmentation, encryption, access control, logging, vulnerability management, payment page script integrity |
| **SOX (ITGC)** | financial reporting integrity | change management, access to financial systems, segregation of duties, evidence |
| **GDPR** | personal data | lawful basis, minimisation, rights (access, erasure), breach notification in 72 hours, privacy by design, DPIAs |
| **ISO 27001** | information security management system | risk management, policies, controls (Annex A), continual improvement |
| **SOC 2** | trust services for service organisations | controls over security, availability, confidentiality, evidence over a period |
| **DORA** | ICT operational resilience (EU financial entities) | ICT risk management, incident classification and reporting, resilience testing (including TLPT), third-party ICT risk, register of providers |

### One control framework
Build a **unified control library** (for example based on ISO 27001 Annex A or NIST CSF) where each control maps to all frameworks requiring it: "production changes are reviewed and deployed by pipelines" satisfies SOX change management, PCI 6.5, ISO A.8.32, SOC 2 CC8.1. Evidence collected once, automatically, reused for all audits (GRC tooling).

### Engineering role
Controls as code (policies, pipelines, tests), automated evidence, architecture decisions that shrink scope (tokenisation, segmentation).

questions.q: You discover that an attacker has had access to a production database replica for an unknown period. Lead the security incident response.
questions.a:
### Immediate (hours)
1. **Declare a security incident**, assemble the team (incident commander, security lead, forensics, legal, privacy officer, communications, executives).
2. **Contain without destroying evidence**: revoke the access path (credentials, keys, network routes), isolate affected systems, snapshot disks and memory, preserve logs (extend retention, copy to immutable storage).
3. Engage external forensics and retain counsel to maintain privilege where appropriate.

### Investigate (days)
- Establish the **attack path** (initial access, persistence, lateral movement), timeline, and data accessed (database audit logs, query logs, network flows, egress volumes).
- Hunt for persistence elsewhere (new identities, keys, scheduled tasks, modified images).
- Determine affected individuals and data categories.

### Notify
- GDPR: supervisory authority within **72 hours** of awareness if risk to individuals; affected individuals without undue delay if high risk.
- DORA major incident reporting timelines; PCI card brand notifications if card data involved; regulators and law enforcement as required.

### Eradicate and recover
Rotate all potentially exposed secrets and keys, rebuild compromised systems from trusted images, close the root cause, increase monitoring.

### Learn
Post-incident review, control improvements (detection gaps, least privilege), board reporting.

  CT --> SC[Scope: logs, queries run, data touched, time window]
  SC --> ER[Eradicate: close entry point, rotate secrets]
  ER --> RC[Recover: rebuild from clean images, monitor closely]
  RC --> NT[Notify: regulators, customers, within legal deadlines]
  NT --> PM[Post-incident review and control fixes]
  SC -.->|in parallel| LG[Legal, privacy, comms]

questions.q: Conduct the security architecture review of a new real-time payments platform before build starts. What do you examine and what outcomes do you require?

### Inputs
Context diagram, data flows, data classification, trust boundaries, third parties (schemes, KYC, fraud vendors), regulatory obligations, availability targets.

| Identity | customer, staff, partner and workload identities; MFA and SCA; token design and binding |
| Authorisation | object-level model, maker-checker, limits, delegated access |
| Data | classification, encryption (at rest, in transit, field level), tokenisation, retention, residency |
| Integrity | message signing with schemes, idempotency, reconciliation, ledger immutability |
| Fraud and abuse | ATO, APP fraud controls, velocity limits, mule detection integration |
| Resilience | DDoS, rate limits, degraded modes, failover without security gaps |
| Supply chain | dependencies, build provenance, vendor security |
| Secrets and keys | KMS, HSM for signing keys, rotation |
| Monitoring | security events, detections, audit trail completeness |
| Operations | privileged access, break-glass, change controls |

### Required outcomes
- Threat model with mitigations mapped to epics.
- Security requirements (ASVS level 2 or 3 for core) in the backlog.
- Decisions recorded as ADRs (token binding, key custody).

questions.q: What is crypto agility, why does post-quantum cryptography matter for a bank now ("harvest now, decrypt later"), and what is your migration roadmap?
questions.a:
### Threat
A cryptographically relevant quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (key exchange and signatures). Symmetric crypto (AES-256) and hashes remain fine with larger parameters. Attackers can **record encrypted traffic today** and decrypt it later: data with long confidentiality needs (customer data, contracts) is already at risk.

### Standards
NIST finalised ML-KEM (Kyber) for key encapsulation and ML-DSA (Dilithium) and SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) for signatures in 2024. Hybrid key exchange (X25519 plus ML-KEM) is being deployed in TLS by browsers and CDNs.

### Crypto agility
The ability to change algorithms and keys without redesign: algorithms configured not hard-coded, versioned ciphertexts and signatures, central crypto services, inventory of where crypto is used.

### Roadmap
1. **Inventory** (cryptographic bill of materials): TLS endpoints, certificates, signing keys, HSMs, libraries, protocols with partners and schemes, data with long confidentiality.
2. **Prioritise** by data lifetime and exposure (external TLS, long-term archives, partner channels).
3. **Agility first**: refactor hard-coded crypto behind services; version formats.
4. **Hybrid TLS** where supported by platforms (CDN, load balancers, .NET as OS libraries add support).
5. Vendor and HSM roadmaps; scheme and regulator timelines.
6. Pilot PQC signatures for internal artefacts; plan certificate hierarchy migration.
pts: Quantum threatens RSA and ECC; symmetric crypto survives.
Harvest now, decrypt later puts long-lived data at risk today.
NIST ML-KEM and ML-DSA standards; hybrid TLS.
Crypto agility: config, versioning, central services, inventory.
Roadmap: inventory, prioritise, agility, hybrid, vendors.
questions.ex: A bank's crypto inventory found 140 hard-coded RSA usages across services and partners, including 25-year document archives encrypted with RSA-wrapped keys. Centralising signing and wrapping behind policy-driven services made the later switch to hybrid schemes a configuration change for most systems.
fu: What is a cryptographic bill of materials?
When will regulators mandate PQC?
What is hybrid key exchange?
pit: Waiting for quantum computers to exist.

questions.q: Build a security champions programme that actually changes engineering behaviour. Structure, incentives and measures.
questions.a:
### Structure
- One champion per team (volunteer, with manager support and 10 to 20% time allocated).
- Onboarding curriculum: threat modelling, OWASP Top 10 and API Top 10, secure code review, the bank's paved roads and tools.
- Monthly guild meetings with real incident and pen test findings; a chat channel with AppSec engineers on call.
- Champions own team-level security practices: threat models, PR reviews of sensitive paths, triage of scanner findings, security backlog hygiene.

### Incentives
Recognition (career framework credit, visible contributions), training budgets and certifications, involvement in red team debriefs and architecture decisions, not extra unpaid work.

### Measures
| Metric | Signal |
|---|---|
| teams with active champions | coverage |
| threat models for significant changes | practice adoption |
| vulnerability SLA compliance per team | outcomes |
| recurrence of bug classes after training | learning |
| champion retention and satisfaction | sustainability |

### Pitfalls
Champions as unpaid security police, programmes without AppSec support, training without follow-through, and measuring attendance instead of outcomes.

questions.q: How do you manage security risk as a principal engineer: identify, assess, decide (mitigate, transfer, accept) and communicate to business leaders?
questions.a:
### Identify
Threat models, pen tests, vulnerability data, architecture reviews, incidents, threat intelligence, audit findings.

### Assess
Likelihood and impact in business terms: customers affected, financial loss, regulatory penalties, downtime. Qualitative matrices are common; **quantitative** approaches (FAIR) estimate loss ranges and help compare investments.

### Decide
| Option | Example |
|---|---|
| Mitigate | add controls (MFA, segmentation) |
| Transfer | insurance, contractual liability with vendors |
| Avoid | don't build the risky feature or change the design |
| Accept | document, time-box, owner signs off with compensating controls |

### Risk acceptance done right
Written statement of the risk, business owner (not an engineer) accepts, expiry date, compensating controls, review on change. Accepted risks visible in a register reported to risk committees.

### Communicating
Lead with business impact and options with costs ("this 3-month change reduces expected loss from X to Y"), avoid jargon, show trends, be honest about uncertainty.

# Risk register entry
risk:
  id: RSK-2026-044
  title: "Legacy statement service lacks object-level authorisation tests"
  scenario: "Authenticated customer enumerates other customers' statements via id manipulation"
  likelihood: medium        # similar issue found by pen test in sister service
  impact: high              # personal data breach, GDPR notification, reputational
  fair_estimate_annual_loss: { p10: 50000, p50: 400000, p90: 3200000 }
  decision: mitigate
  mitigation: { owner: team-statements, actions: [resource-based authz, BOLA tests], due: 2026-11-30 }
  interim_compensating_controls: [WAF rate rule on statement ids, detection for sequential id access]
  accepted_by: null
  review: 2026-12-15
~~~

Assess in business terms; FAIR for quantification.
Mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept.
Acceptance by business owners with expiry and compensating controls.
Communicate impact and options with costs.
